stimulus.source_note: Map of the United States, the Area of Freedom and Slavery, and the Territories Whose Destiny Is Yet to Be Decided (G. W. Elliott, New York, 1856). Republican campaign broadside map; portraits of John C. Frémont and William L. Dayton. Library of Congress, African American Odyssey exhibit; Cornell University Library, RMC2008_0909. Public domain.
stimulus.text: A Republican campaign map published in New York in 1856, titled “Map of the United States, the Area of Freedom and Slavery, and the Territories Whose Destiny Is Yet to Be Decided.” Portraits of John C. Frémont and William L. Dayton stand at the top corners. The free states are colored pink, the slave states gray, and the western territories pale yellow, with a heavy black line marking the Missouri Compromise line at 36°30′. Tables at the foot compare the free and slave states by population, wealth, and railroads, using the census of 1850.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note

rationales.A: The map shows Frémont’s western routes, but its portraits and title are about the 1856 election, not Lewis and Clark.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Texas had been annexed in 1845, eleven years before this map; the map is about the territories’ future, not Texas.
rationales.C: Frémont’s portrait crowns a map whose whole argument is free soil against slave soil, tying the candidate to the territories’ fate.
rationales.D: The map marks Frémont’s exploration routes, but it argues about slavery, not about where to build a railroad.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the top: the portraits name the Republican ticket, Frémont and Dayton.
2. Read the title: the map divides the country into freedom and slavery, with territories still undecided.
3. See the pitch: the map sells Frémont as the man for the free-soil side of that divide.
Remember: on a campaign map, the portraits tell you whose argument the geography is making.
